title: The Sovereign Citizen Movement in the United States
summary: ADL report on the US sovereign citizen movement: origins, gurus, Moorish variant, paper terrorism, scams, violence, and post-2020 growth at home and abroad.

assertions.quote: evolved from ideas originally pioneered by two older anti-government movements, the tax protest movement and the Posse Comitatus movement
One of the most popular paper terrorism tactics is also one of the very oldest: the bogus lien.
Sovereign citizen gurus hold seminars around the country and online, compose filings and instruction manuals
fueled by another serious recession and the mortgage crisis
Traffic stops are among the most dangerous situations for police officers dealing with sovereign citizens.
often look like checks or money orders, but are entirely worthless, no matter the monetary amount that appears on the documents
produced their own local sovereign citizen gurus who adapted sovereign ideas to the history and laws of the countries where they resided
Most high-profile sovereign citizen influencers of the 2010s ended up behind bars before the end of the decade.

verdicts.note: Many prominent promoters received long prison sentences, though many smaller sellers are never charged.
The redemption promoter the plaintiff followed was convicted of fraud along with followers, and the judge warns that people frequently go to prison for these schemes; this is one guru, not a rate.
Tucci-Jarraf was convicted of bank fraud and a Detaxer guru got 2.5 years for teaching pseudolaw, but other gurus here were convicted of unrelated offences or only declared vexatious; no rate given.
Many promoters of untaxing and pseudolegal tax schemes were convicted (Meredith 121 months, Ambort 108 months, Schiff 12+ years, eight trust promoters in Scott); this is a case list, not a rate.

Elvick was twice imprisoned for fraudulent tax-filing schemes and others were fined or convicted for tax offences or a Ponzi scheme, but many guru convictions were for unrelated crimes (drugs, weapons, sex offences).
A guru behind the Fiscal Arbitrators scheme got six years for fraud and another lost his accounting licence, but the study gives no conviction rate for gurus.
FBI cites convictions of sovereign-citizen sellers of a fake insurance scheme and of phony diplomatic IDs, plus money-laundering arrests; these are examples, not a rate.

assertions.quote: appealing to new audiences, including anti-vaxxers, QAnon adherents, and MAGA supporters

verdicts.note: Monitoring groups documented heavy crossover since 2020, though membership counts are estimates.
Trackers report an upsurge with Covid, with estimates rising to 500,000 in 2022 (methodology questionable), and QAnon links appear in the antipodes; MAGA recruiting is not addressed.

assertions.quote: inmates in jails and prisons, which have become one of the most significant conduits through which sovereign citizen ideology spreads
the most common type of group is the fictitious entity group

verdicts.note: Common-law courts, assemblies and fake police agencies are well documented and have no legal standing.
Groups set up vigilante police ('Territorial Marshals', C3POs) and 'Tacit Supreme in Law' courts claiming jurisdiction superior to the government's.
The 1990s common-law court movement set up its own 'courts' that indict and try officials in absentia, and many are instruments of harassment.
FBI reports sovereign citizens convene their own special courts that issue fake but realistic-looking indictments and warrants, and sell fake licences, passports and law-enforcement credentials.

assertions.quote: sovereign citizen claims and theories are typically little more than meaningless nonsense
